source: You're a monster and a fool. You hideous little man.
You can never understand what you've stolen from me. Never.
(I'm too late. They were already destroyed this time.)
I will not, my Prince. I serve your father above any other man.
I promised your father I would burn the contents of this chest, and I am not about to forego such a promise. I apologize sincerely.
You will not destroy them.
(Oh, my God. His head is in the flames!)
T-that was-- What I just did--
He's dead. It's done.
Now I can take what is rightfully mine.
You murdered him.
Don't try to stop me, Ophelia. You brought this on us. On both of us.
The chest is unlocked. There's parchment inside.
This is his handwriting.
T-this is... this can't be real.
This is a farce. A lie. It must be.
Father wouldn't  write something like this.
What can those notes possibly say, to make him react like that?
Ah. Hello, Othello.
Have you any need to buy a little barley-wine today? I've three casks outside.
A 'little!' Hah. You know this place. The field-fellows drank it all within the first three days.
If you can sell me thrice as much, I can pay it.
Aye. That's well enough.
A drink before you unpack? I'm in no hurry.
I'll indulge these bones a while, yes.
Oh. Ophelia. You're here.
Do you know what today is?
Of course. It's the day you and Mother were first wed.
T-that's right. I'm... surprised you know.
I miss her so very much, Ophelia.
I know, Father.
I'm not certain what you mean. Judging by where we are, I'd assume it's got something to do with Mother?
Today marks the day your mother and I were first wed.
She was close to your age then. We were so very—so wonderfully young. I wish I could remember my own mind at that point in my life.
Everything was so clean and simple, and matters so easy to sort through.
Do you ever miss your mother?
I... think so.
You were so small when Elise died. Hardly able to move on your own. And sickly, too. She was terrified she'd lose you as she lay ill.
She handed you to a nursemaid instead of continuing to feed you. It likely saved your life, though it brought her immense pain to do.
I'm lucky, then.
Your mother was the light of my life.
When she left us, my life—well—I have you, and Laertes. Were it not for you two, my world would have gone completely dark.
For many years it was as though nothing would ever make me smile again. My hair grew white, and my hands feeble. I felt I needed her to live.
You are the spitting image of her. Sometimes, when you were small, I could hardly bear to look at your face. It was too painful.
But I know she'd be so terribly, terribly proud of you and Laertes.
That's what has kept me alive these many years.
Father, I'm sorry to ask now, but what do you know about Queen Astrid and Mother's relationship?
I'll stay out here just a little longer, I think.
If there is anything more you'd like to know about your mother, you have only to ask.
It's difficult remembering. But important.
Father, you know how deeply I love you, right?
I do. I have often felt I was failing my family as of late, most of all you.
I understand that you love me, too.
That brings me some small relief.
I'll leave you be. Be safe, Father.
Oh, Elise.
I miss you in every waking morning and every evening's fire.
It smells like old cloth and parchment in here.
Looks like nothing's been touched in years.
Why is it that Hamlet gets to speak with his father's spirit, but my mother is gone from me without a word?
How can that be fair? Is their presence, their worth, not equal?
There must be something of hers here. Father told me...
This place is as melancholy as ever.
And dusty, too.
I'd better make my business here quickly, and go.
Your mother was close with the Queen, during her service to her. Certain events transpired which no King since would want to come to light.
But you could read about them—if you so desired.
There's something I've never told you before. Something you won't like, I think, and your brother would like even less. But it's the truth.
When she took ill, King Hamlet ordered her put into one of the sanitariums on the southern coast.
Y-you mean the ones far from here? She died... like that?
The King was not kind to her, and would not let her convalesce within the castle along with the rest of the noble-affiliated victims.
He never treated her with kindness, though he was kind to other noblewomen of similar rank.
Because she was foreign-born, you mean.
Yes. Her only crime was being born into a world that could not understand her worth.
The Guard Captain at the time, Bernardo's father, was ordered to prevent me from seeing her. The King feared I would take ill, too, and leave him with no advisor.
I wasn't able to say goodbye.
How could someone do something like that? If she'd been in the sanitarium—she might be—alive!
We both knew when we fell in love that it would end like this. It could be no other way.
I'm a man of the present. I don't like to remember. Painful memories tend to linger and grasp at us far past their right.
But—if you were so inclined—she left behind some notes, composed at the very end of her life.
When she died, some kind soul sent her belongings back to me on a ship. But it was simply too painful for me to dream of looking through them.
They're located in that shack by the docks. They're locked off, along with the other belongings of those who fall to the plague. You'll need to find a way in.
Hardly anyone in the castle will go in there. It's a bad omen. But you're sharp as your mother was. I'm sure you'll find a way.
So good of you to come.
You know, I had expected you much earlier. You've been awfully tardy on this front, haven't you?
...On what front?
I felt certain from the moment we met you would come find me like this. But you haven't. And now—here we are.
I do so love this gallery. King Claudius may be a buffoon, but King Hamlet loved the great dramas and tragedies.
There are even type-printed copies on these shelves. There's something so relaxing about a deep, bloody drama.
Not me. I prefer to read happier tales.
Stories can be beautiful without being happy, don't you think?
Here. Ovid's 'Pyramus et Thisbe', the greatest love story ever written—for now, of course, until some half-rate bard steals and replicates it!
'Alas! Only death could take you from me; therefore, let us not be parted by death.'
Two young lovers, so deeply fallen into one another that they'd rather die gruesomely than live apart.
Don't you think that's beautiful?
You have a funny definition of 'beautiful'. I'd rather see them alive and well.
Death is never the ideal solution. Not for me.
Ahh. You're a woman all about solutions, aren't you? I knew you were a bright girl.
Unfortunate things happen to bright girls in this world.
Why did you really ask me to come here, Quince? What do you want?
Indeed... what do I want? A larger question for another world. But for now...
I'm going to give you the ability to change the content of the play I perform.
If you have any juicy gossip you'd like to see on stage, you need only ask.
Terribly generous of me at this late point in our match—I know, I know!
That's all?
What more were you expecting? Adieu, Lady Ophelia.
My dear, what a funny little play you wove for me.
And a desperate one, at that.
I don't expect they'll understand.
A word of advice, Lady Ophelia, if I may be so bold. Don't ask the others to try and understand what you and I are.
Can the insects on the floor of the great hall understand the intelligence of humans who walk above them? Certainly not!
No more can the men and women of Elsinore understand the rules governing our current predicament.
They will only shun you for it.
You're saying they'll never believe me?
That is correct, yes. They are fundamentally incapable of it. Now, if you'll excuse me.
I find myself both unamused and overtaxed. The worst of both worlds.
Now, are you going to return to making a choice, or shall we play this tedious back-and-forth longer?
I don't much care for it, I must admit.
If you'll excuse me, I'll take my leave of you now.
I do wish you'd find something else to perform. You won't glean any information from me repeating this same rehashed tale.
Wait a minute. I'm not done with you.
I am done with you.
Ah, there you are.
His Majesty and Bernardo are already inside. I'll open the door. You will enter after me and remain concealed. When you sense the meeting is over, depart before us.
Say and do nothing. Do you understand?
Captain. I was the one who asked Claudius to call this meeting.
And you as well, I suppose.
Let's just say I have the King's ear for the time being.
Aah-- I see.
Well, then, my lady, please, take caution. Conceal yourself and make no noise or word.
His Majesty would certainly not appreciate me allowing a lady of the court into a meeting like this.
I'll merely listen and remain concealed. My thanks, Bernardo.
Captain. My father told me this meeting was taking place.
As did you, I suppose.
And if I promise to stay concealed?
This is important, Bernardo. I won't give myself away. I promise.
I don't know what this is all about. But given you seem rather intent, I'll permit it this one time. Make no noise or word.
My lord? Are you present?
My King, good Captain, I convened this council for good reason.
I believe circumstances have shifted beneath our feet. We must be compelled to act now, or lose everything.
Your Highness. In short, we are in danger.
Your Highness. What is this about?
I have new cause to believe we are in danger, Bernardo.
Is this about Ophelia's little rumormongering?
Rumormongering, sir?
What rumors, my lord?
She came to me trying to peddle some little words about Fortinbras hiding out nearby.
Did Ophelia come to you with this?
She's been saying something of the sort lately. That's all.
A-ah, my lord, that was... that is to say... she was only repeating what I've told her.
She's parroting what I have already learned via our usual warfront network, of course.
She did?
